Applied Bayesian Inference · Chapter 6

Chapter 6
Multilevel models

Lectures 11–12 · partial pooling, empirical Bayes, varying slopes, the geometry of hierarchies, and ambulance response times across New York

Data almost always come in groups: patients in hospitals, students in schools, neighbourhoods in boroughs, measurements of the same country over many years. The groups differ, and they differ in size. A few have hundreds of observations and some have one. How should we estimate each group's average? We could treat every group as unrelated to every other, trusting each group's own data entirely. We could ignore the groups and use one overall average for all of them. Or we could do something in between: estimate each group's average, but let the groups inform each other, so that groups with little data borrow strength from the rest.

The third option is the multilevel model (also called a hierarchical or mixed-effects model), and it is probably the single most useful technique in applied Bayesian statistics. It treats the group averages as themselves drawn from a population, learns from the data how much the groups differ, and pulls each group's estimate toward the population average by exactly the amount its own data warrant. Groups with lots of data barely move; groups with little data move a lot. This shrinkage sounds like a compromise, but it is not: shrunken estimates are, on average, more accurate than the raw group averages. That fact so surprised statisticians when it was proved in the 1950s that it became known as a paradox.

  • Lecture 11 is about pooling. We will ask which country grows the best coffee, using ratings of 1,309 coffees from 36 countries, see why the raw rankings mislead, fit a multilevel model, check on held-out data that its estimates predict better, and meet empirical Bayes: the shortcut that estimates the population from the data and the history of Stein's paradox.
  • Lecture 12 extends the idea. Groups can differ in their slopes as well as their averages: we will model how carbon emissions per person changed in 164 countries from 2000 to 2022, and ask whether richer countries cut them faster. Then we confront the computational price of hierarchies, the funnel, and the reparameterisation that removes it, and end with a case study from New York City's ambulance dispatch records: response times to cardiac arrests across nearly 200 ZIP codes.

Think About It: Before You Start

In the 1990s and 2000s, several large foundations in the United States spent billions of dollars breaking big high schools into small ones, partly because the schools with the highest average test scores were disproportionately small. What else would you expect to find if you looked at the schools with the lowest average scores? Write down your prediction; the history box in Section 6.1 tells you what happened.

Lecture 11 — Pooling

6.1 Many small groups: which country grows the best coffee?

The Coffee Quality Institute trains and certifies professional tasters ("Q graders") who score green coffee beans on a 100-point scale, adding up marks for aroma, flavour, aftertaste, acidity, body, balance and other attributes. In 2018 the data scientist James LeDoux collected the institute's public reviews of more than 1,300 coffees, and the data were later shared through the TidyTuesday project. We keep the 1,309 Arabica coffees that have a country of origin and a valid score (one record has a score of zero) and ask a simple question: which country produces the best coffee?

R
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(posterior)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

harbour <- c(ink = "#10191d", muted = "#4a5f68", grid = "#d5e3e6",
             sky = "#1d5187", amber = "#805907", rose = "#ad3b28",
             moss = "#1d6b54", lilac = "#5b3a94")
theme_harbour <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = harbour[["ink"]]),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = harbour[["muted"]]),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = harbour[["grid"]]),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(colour = harbour[["ink"]], hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "top")
}
theme_set(theme_harbour())
R
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2020/2020-07-07/coffee_ratings.csv"
coffee <- read_csv(url, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(species == "Arabica", total_cup_points > 50, !is.na(country_of_origin)) |>
  transmute(country = country_of_origin, score = total_cup_points, method = processing_method)
nrow(coffee); n_distinct(coffee$country)

by_country <- coffee |> group_by(country) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(score))
by_country |> arrange(-mean) |> head(6)          # the raw "top six"
by_country |> arrange(mean) |> head(4)           # and the bottom four
output
[1] 1309
[1] 36
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  country              n  mean
  <chr>            <int> <dbl>
1 United States        8  86.0
2 Papua New Guinea     1  85.8
3 Ethiopia            44  85.5
4 Japan                1  84.7
5 Kenya               25  84.3
6 Uganda              26  84.1
# A tibble: 4 x 3
  country           n  mean
  <chr>         <int> <dbl>
1 India             1  76.8
2 Haiti             6  77.2
3 Cote d?Ivoire     1  79.3
4 Nicaragua        26  80.5

The raw ranking puts the United States first (8 coffees, average 86.0), then Papua New Guinea, represented by a single coffee, then Ethiopia (44 coffees averaging 85.5) and Japan (again a single coffee). At the bottom are India (one coffee), Haiti (six) and Côte d'Ivoire (one). Would you bet that Papua New Guinea grows better coffee than Ethiopia on the strength of one bag? The top and bottom of a ranking of raw averages are dominated by small groups, for the simplest of reasons: the average of a few observations is noisy, and noise pushes some small groups far above the truth and others far below it.

History: The Most Dangerous Equation

In 2007 the statistician Howard Wainer called de Moivre's formula for the standard error of a mean, σ/n, "the most dangerous equation", because ignorance of it has cost so much. His leading example was the small-schools movement. Analyses of Pennsylvania test scores had found that small schools were heavily over-represented among the best-performing schools, and foundations including the Gates Foundation invested heavily in creating smaller schools. But small schools were also over-represented among the worst-performing schools, as σ/n predicts: averages over fewer students are more variable in both directions. The same trap appears in maps of cancer rates by county (the highest and lowest rates are in thinly populated rural counties), in hospital league tables and in restaurant ratings. Every one of these is a problem for a multilevel model.

6.2 Three ways to pool

Write yij for the score of coffee i from country j. Three models are possible, and they differ only in what they assume about the country averages αj.

  • Complete pooling assumes all countries are the same: yij∼Normal(α,σ) with a single α. It ignores real differences between countries.
  • No pooling assumes the countries have nothing to do with each other: each αj gets its own fixed prior, and its estimate is essentially the country's own average. It treats one coffee from Japan as if it told us all about Japanese coffee.
  • Partial pooling assumes the countries are different but related: their averages are drawn from a common population, αj∼Normal(μ,τ), where μ is the average of the country averages and τ how much they differ. Crucially, μ and τ are parameters, estimated from the data along with everything else.

The partial-pooling model is a multilevel model because it has two levels of variation: coffees vary around their country's average (with standard deviation σ), and countries vary around the population average (with standard deviation τ). The prior for each αj is not fixed in advance; it is learned from the other countries. In full:

yij∼Normal(αj,σ)
αj∼Normal(μ,τ)
μ∼Normal(82,5),τ∼Exponential(1),σ∼Exponential(0.5).

When σ, μ and τ are known, each country's posterior mean has a simple and revealing form:

α^j=wjy¯j+(1−wj)μ,wj=τ2τ2+σ2/nj.

The estimate is a weighted average of the country's own mean and the population mean. The weight on the country's own data, wj, compares how much countries genuinely differ (τ2) with how noisy the country's own average is (σ2/nj). With many coffees, σ2/nj is small, wj is near 1, and the country keeps its own average. With one coffee, wj may be well below one-half and the estimate is pulled most of the way to the population mean. Complete pooling is the case τ=0; no pooling is τ=∞. The widget lets you set τ by hand.

From no pooling to complete pooling

Each country's estimate (dot) against its number of coffees (log scale), with a line from its raw average (open circle). Set τ, the spread between countries; σ is fixed at the within-country standard deviation, 2.4 points, and μ at its best-fitting value for that τ. The readout gives the top three, and the error of these estimates when the coffees are split in two at random and the estimates from one half predict the averages in the other (averaged over 50 random splits; see Section 6.4).

At τ near zero, every country gets the overall average: no country is better than any other. At very large τ, every country keeps its raw average, and the one-coffee countries sit at the extremes. In between, the large countries barely move while the small ones slide toward the centre, and the ranking changes: at the estimated τ, Ethiopia, the United States and Kenya are the top three, Papua New Guinea drops from second to fifth, and Japan falls into the pack. Watch the held-out error as you move the slider. It is large at both ends and smallest somewhere in the middle, near the value of τ that the multilevel model estimates from the data.

Check Yourself

Suppose τ=1.4 points and σ=2.4 points. What weight wj does a country with a single coffee give to its own average?

wj=τ2/(τ2+σ2/nj) with nj=1.

w=1.42/(1.42+2.42)=1.96/(1.96+5.76)=0.25. One coffee earns a quarter of the weight; three-quarters of the estimate comes from the population of countries.

6.3 Fitting a multilevel model

In brms, a varying intercept is written (1 | country): "an intercept that varies by country". The standard deviation of the country intercepts, τ, is a parameter of class sd.

R
m_coffee <- brm(score ~ 1 + (1 | country), data = coffee,
                prior = c(prior(normal(82, 5), class = Intercept),
                          prior(exponential(1), class = sd),          # tau: spread between countries
                          prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma)),    # spread within countries
                seed = 6, refresh = 0, file = "fits/ch6_coffee")
summary(m_coffee)
output

         total post-warmup draws = 4000

~country (Number of levels: 36) 
              Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS

Population-Level Effects: 
          Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS

The summary has the familiar Intercept (now μ, about 82.3 points) and sigma (2.4 points of variation between coffees from the same country), and a new block, Group-Level Effects (called Multilevel Hyperparameters in recent versions of brms), reporting sd(Intercept): τ, the standard deviation of the true country averages, about 1.4 points with a 95% interval of roughly 1.0 to 2.0. Countries differ, but by less than individual coffees within a country do. A common summary is the intraclass correlation, τ2/(τ2+σ2): the share of the variation in scores that lies between countries, here about a quarter.

R
est <- coef(m_coffee)$country[, , "Intercept"] |> as_tibble(rownames = "country") |>
  left_join(by_country, by = "country")
mu_hat <- fixef(m_coffee)["Intercept", "Estimate"]
ggplot(est, aes(n)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mu_hat, linetype = "dashed", colour = harbour[["muted"]]) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n, y = mean, yend = Estimate), colour = harbour[["muted"]], alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean), shape = 1, colour = harbour[["rose"]], size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Estimate), colour = harbour[["sky"]], size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "number of coffees (log scale)", y = "average score")

The figure is the whole chapter in one picture. On the right, Mexico, Colombia and Guatemala, with well over a hundred coffees each, are estimated at essentially their own averages. On the left, the one-coffee countries are pulled about three-quarters of the way to the population mean (the weight from Check 6.1). Haiti, whose six coffees averaged 77.2, the lowest of any country, is moved up by more than a point; the United States, at the top with eight, is moved down by almost one.

A ranking should carry its uncertainty. With posterior draws of every country's average, we can compute, for each draw, which country comes first, and report the share of draws in which each country is best: the posterior probability of being the best.

R
draws_c <- coef(m_coffee, summary = FALSE)$country[, , "Intercept"]   # draws x countries
best <- colnames(draws_c)[apply(draws_c, 1, which.max)]
tibble(country = best) |> count(country, name = "draws") |>
  mutate(`Pr(best)` = draws / nrow(draws_c)) |> arrange(-draws) |> head(6)
output
# A tibble: 6 x 3
  country          draws `Pr(best)`
  <chr>            <int>      <dbl>
1 Ethiopia          2247     0.562 
2 United States     1224     0.306 
3 Papua New Guinea   181     0.0452
4 Japan              107     0.0268
5 Ecuador             63     0.0158
6 Rwanda              44     0.011

Ethiopia is the best coffee-producing country in a little over half the posterior draws and the United States in about 30%; no other country reaches 5%. Papua New Guinea and Japan, second and fourth on raw averages, come first in under 5% and 3% of draws. "Ethiopia probably, possibly the United States (on the evidence of eight coffees, mostly from Hawaii), and we cannot tell beyond that" is a far more honest conclusion than a league table.

Research Practice: Rank with Uncertainty, or Not at All

Rankings of hospitals, schools, neighbourhoods, police precincts and universities are published constantly, and most are rankings of raw rates. A publishable analysis should: estimate group rates with a multilevel model, so that small groups are not ranked first or last by luck; report the posterior distribution of each group's rank, or the probability of being in the top (or bottom) k, rather than a single ordering; and state how many groups are statistically distinguishable at all. Goldstein and Spiegelhalter (1996) made this argument for school and hospital league tables, and it remains one of the most useful contributions a statistician can make to public debate.

6.4 Does pooling predict better?

The claim that shrunken estimates are more accurate is testable. Split every country's coffees into two random halves. Estimate each country's average from the first half, in three ways (no pooling, complete pooling and partial pooling), and see which estimates come closest to the average of the other half.

R
set.seed(6)
coffee <- coffee |> group_by(country) |>
  mutate(half = sample(rep(1:2, length.out = n()))) |> ungroup()
first  <- filter(coffee, half == 1)
second <- coffee |> filter(half == 2) |> group_by(country) |> summarise(n2 = n(), target = mean(score))

m_half <- update(m_coffee, newdata = first, seed = 6, refresh = 0)
predictions <- first |> group_by(country) |> summarise(n1 = n(), `no pooling` = mean(score)) |>
  mutate(`complete pooling` = fixef(m_half)["Intercept", "Estimate"],
         `partial pooling` = coef(m_half)$country[country, "Estimate", "Intercept"])
predictions |> inner_join(second, by = "country") |>
  pivot_longer(c(`no pooling`, `complete pooling`, `partial pooling`), names_to = "method") |>
  group_by(method) |> summarise(countries = n(), mse = mean((value - target)^2)) |> arrange(mse)
output
# A tibble: 3 x 3
  method           countries   mse
  <chr>                <int> <dbl>
1 no pooling              28  1.49
2 partial pooling         28  1.63
3 complete pooling        28  3.38

A surprise: in this split, the raw averages (no pooling) predicted the other half slightly better than the multilevel estimates, although both beat complete pooling by a wide margin. Is shrinkage a fraud? No. Stein's result, which we meet in the next section, is about expected error, averaged over the noise; any single split is one draw of that noise, and here a couple of small countries happened to have first-half averages that their second halves agreed with. The honest test repeats the split many times. Refitting brms two hundred times would take a while, so the loop below uses lme4::lmer, the fast non-Bayesian fit of the same varying-intercept model, which with 36 countries gives nearly identical estimates.

R
library(lme4)
one_split <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  d <- coffee |> group_by(country) |> mutate(half = sample(rep(1:2, length.out = n()))) |> ungroup()
  fit <- lmer(score ~ 1 + (1 | country), data = filter(d, half == 1))
  est <- coef(fit)$country |> as_tibble(rownames = "country") |> rename(partial = `(Intercept)`)
  d |> filter(half == 1) |> group_by(country) |> summarise(n1 = n(), raw = mean(score)) |>
    mutate(complete = fixef(fit)[[1]]) |> left_join(est, by = "country") |>
    inner_join(d |> filter(half == 2) |> group_by(country) |> summarise(target = mean(score)), by = "country") |>
    mutate(split = seed)
}
splits <- map_dfr(1:200, one_split)
mse <- splits |> group_by(split) |>
  summarise(across(c(raw, complete, partial), ~ mean((.x - target)^2)))
mse |> summarise(`Pr(partial beats raw)` = mean(partial < raw), across(c(raw, complete, partial), mean))
output
# A tibble: 1 x 4
  `Pr(partial beats raw)`   raw complete partial
                    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1                    0.75  2.52     3.38    2.01

Averaged over 200 random splits, partial pooling has the lowest error: about a fifth lower than the raw averages and less than two-thirds that of complete pooling, and it beats the raw averages in roughly three splits out of four. Neither extreme is a good idea; borrowing strength by the right amount is. And note what "the right amount" was: no one chose it. The model estimated τ from the data, and τ determined how much each country borrowed. The widget in Section 6.2 reports this same average over 50 of the splits, so you can watch the error change with τ.

Check Yourself

Why does the multilevel estimate for a one-coffee country predict that country's other coffees better than the coffee's own score does?

Shrinkage pulls toward the population mean; it does not add data from that country.

Shrinkage is a weighted average, not a correction for bias in the raw data.

The raw average of one coffee is unbiased but has a large variance (σ2=5.8 squared points). Shrinking it toward μ introduces a little bias but removes most of the variance, so the expected squared error falls. This bias-variance trade-off is the heart of Stein's result.

Because a single score is a very noisy estimate of the country's average, and pulling it toward the population mean reduces that noise more than it adds bias.

6.5 Empirical Bayes

The multilevel model treats μ and τ as unknown parameters with priors, and integrates over them. An older and simpler approach, called empirical Bayes, instead estimates them from the data, plugs the estimates in, and then applies Bayes' rule to each group with that estimated prior. The estimates come from the marginal likelihood: the probability of the observed group averages with the group effects integrated out. For our model, each country's observed average is normally distributed around μ with variance τ2+σ2/nj (true variation plus sampling noise), so

(μ^,τ^)=argmaxμ,τ∏jNormal(y¯j|μ, τ2+σ2/nj).

This is also called type-II maximum likelihood, or evidence maximisation. It is a few lines of R.

R
sigma_w <- coffee |> group_by(country) |> mutate(dev = score - mean(score)) |> pull(dev) |> sd()
marg_ll <- function(par, d) {                    # log marginal likelihood of the country averages
  mu <- par[1]; tau <- exp(par[2])
  sum(dnorm(d$mean, mu, sqrt(tau^2 + sigma_w^2 / d$n), log = TRUE))
}
fit_eb <- optim(c(82, 0), marg_ll, d = by_country, control = list(fnscale = -1))
c(sigma_within = sigma_w, mu_hat = fit_eb$par[1], tau_hat = exp(fit_eb$par[2]))
posterior_summary(m_coffee, variable = c("b_Intercept", "sd_country__Intercept"))   # full Bayes
output
sigma_within       mu_hat      tau_hat 
       2.407       82.305        1.412 
                      Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5  Q97.5
b_Intercept             82.307    0.2942 81.733 82.890
sd_country__Intercept    1.443    0.2408  1.024  1.966

Empirical Bayes estimates τ^≈1.4 points, the same as the multilevel model's posterior mean, and its shrunken country averages are almost identical to the full Bayesian ones. With 36 countries, the data pin down τ well, and plugging in a single value loses little. Empirical Bayes is fast, transparent and widely used in genomics (estimating thousands of gene-level variances at once), in sports and insurance analytics, and in disease mapping.

History: Stein's Paradox

In 1956 Charles Stein, at Stanford, proved something that most statisticians refused to believe. When estimating three or more means at once (say, the true averages of several unrelated groups), the obvious estimate, each group's own sample average, is inadmissible: there is another estimate that has lower total squared error for every possible value of the true means. In 1961 Stein and his student Willard James gave it explicitly: shrink every sample average toward the grand mean by a factor estimated from the data. The James–Stein estimator is exactly the empirical Bayes estimate above. Herbert Robbins had developed "empirical Bayes" methods independently in 1956. The idea reached a wide audience through Bradley Efron and Carl Morris, whose 1977 Scientific American article "Stein's paradox in statistics" showed it at work on real problems, including the prevalence of toxoplasmosis in 36 cities of El Salvador (Efron and Morris, 1975): the cities with the most extreme observed rates were mostly the smallest. What looked paradoxical from a frequentist viewpoint is natural from a Bayesian one: the groups are related, so each one's data are informative about the others.

Empirical Bayes has one weakness, and it matters most when groups are few. By plugging in τ^ as if it were known, it ignores the uncertainty in τ, so its intervals for the group effects are too narrow. When the data pin τ down, that hardly matters. When they do not, a single number hides the fact that the data are consistent both with "these groups are identical" and with "they differ a lot"; and with few groups the maximum-likelihood estimate is often exactly zero, which forces complete pooling with complete confidence. The widget shows the marginal likelihood for τ with all 36 countries, and with only the eight countries represented by a single coffee.

How much do the data say about τ?

The marginal (type-II) likelihood of τ, maximised over μ at each value of τ and scaled so its peak is 1. Empirical Bayes uses the peak; full Bayes multiplies the whole curve by a prior and keeps all of it.

With all 36 countries, the likelihood is a well-defined hump around 1.4. With only the eight one-coffee countries it still peaks near 1.4, but it is almost flat from zero to beyond 3: eight noisy scores cannot tell "these countries are identical" from "they differ by three points". Here is what the two approaches conclude from those eight countries alone.

R
one <- by_country |> filter(n == 1) |> mutate(se = sigma_w)        # eight countries, one coffee each
fit_eb8 <- optim(c(82, 0), marg_ll, d = one, control = list(fnscale = -1))
c(mu_hat = fit_eb8$par[1], tau_hat = exp(fit_eb8$par[2]))

m_one <- brm(mean | se(se) ~ 1 + (1 | country), data = one,            # known measurement error
             prior = c(prior(normal(82, 5), class = Intercept), prior(exponential(1), class = sd)),
             seed = 6, refresh = 0, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), file = "fits/ch6_one")
posterior_summary(m_one, variable = "sd_country__Intercept")
coef(m_one)$country[, , "Intercept"] |> round(2)
output
 mu_hat tau_hat 
 81.958   1.369 
                      Estimate Est.Error    Q2.5 Q97.5
sd_country__Intercept   0.9511    0.8266 0.02546  3.03
                 Estimate Est.Error  Q2.5 Q97.5
Cote d?Ivoire       81.54      1.34 78.55 83.92
Ecuador             82.25      1.27 80.01 85.17
India               81.13      1.56 77.36 83.63
Japan               82.38      1.34 80.04 85.53
Mauritius           81.70      1.25 78.95 83.98
Papua New Guinea    82.57      1.39 80.23 86.03
Rwanda              82.10      1.26 79.76 84.72
Zambia              81.97      1.23 79.58 84.50

Empirical Bayes reports τ^≈1.4 and proceeds as if that were known. The full Bayesian 95% interval for τ runs from almost zero to about 3, with posterior mean about 0.95 (the exponential prior pulls gently toward smaller values). The eight country estimates are shrunk hard toward about 82, each with an interval 5 to 6 points wide that averages over every plausible τ. With a slightly different eight countries the empirical Bayes estimate could as easily have been 0 or 2.5, and every downstream interval would have inherited that accident. The formula mean | se(se) tells brms that each observation is itself an estimate with a known standard error: the syntax of a Bayesian meta-analysis, which is exactly this model applied to the results of several studies.

Research Practice: Full Bayes with Few Groups

Use empirical Bayes freely when there are many groups (dozens or more) and computation is expensive; report τ^ and check that a full Bayesian fit agrees on a subset. With fewer than about ten groups, use full Bayes, put a weakly informative prior on τ (a half-normal or exponential scaled to the plausible size of group differences), and report how the conclusions depend on it, because the data alone cannot determine τ. This is the standard situation in meta-analysis of a handful of trials, in multi-site studies with few sites, and in comparisons of a few boroughs or departments.

Check Yourself

Ignoring uncertainty in τ does not make intervals wider.

Compare with the full Bayesian intervals.

Plugging in τ^=0 forces complete pooling and treats it as certain. The full Bayesian posterior keeps the plausible values of τ above zero, which widens each group's interval to include genuine differences between groups.

too narrow, because it treats τ = 0 as known when values up to about 3 are plausible

Key Takeaways: Lecture 11

  • Raw group averages put small groups at the extremes by chance; rankings of raw rates mislead.
  • A multilevel model treats group effects as draws from a population with spread τ, learned from the data. Each group's estimate is a weighted average of its own data and the population mean.
  • Shrunken estimates predict better than raw averages or a single pooled mean, as the held-out test showed.
  • Report rankings as posterior probabilities, not league tables.
  • Empirical Bayes estimates τ by maximising the marginal likelihood; it matches full Bayes with many groups but is overconfident with few.

Lecture 12 — Slopes, levels and geometry

6.6 Varying slopes: carbon emissions in 164 countries

Groups can differ in more than their averages. When the same units are measured repeatedly over time, each unit has its own trend, and the trends differ too. Our example is a question at the centre of climate policy. Between 2000 and 2022, did emissions of carbon dioxide per person fall in rich countries and rise in poorer ones, and how much do countries at the same income level differ? The data come from Our World in Data, which compiles territorial (production-based) emissions from the Global Carbon Project (Friedlingstein et al., 2023) and national accounts.

R
url_co2 <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/co2-data/master/owid-co2-data.csv"
owid <- read_csv(url_co2, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(nchar(iso_code) == 3, !startsWith(iso_code, "OWID"), between(year, 2000, 2022))  # countries only
gdp2000 <- owid |> filter(year == 2000, !is.na(gdp)) |>
  transmute(country, log_gdp = log(gdp / population))                                     # GDP per person in 2000
co2 <- owid |> filter(co2_per_capita > 0) |>
  inner_join(gdp2000, by = "country") |>
  group_by(country) |> filter(n() == 23) |> ungroup() |>                                  # complete series only
  mutate(y = log(co2_per_capita),                 # log tonnes of CO2 per person
         t = (year - 2010) / 10,                  # decades from 2010
         g = log_gdp - mean(gdp2000$log_gdp))     # centred log GDP per person in 2000
c(countries = n_distinct(co2$country), rows = nrow(co2))
output
countries      rows 
      164      3772

Each country j now gets its own intercept aj (its log emissions per person in 2010) and its own slope bj (the change in log emissions per decade; a slope of −0.1 means about a 10% fall per decade). Both depend on the country's income in 2000, and each country deviates from that dependence by its own amount:

yjt∼Normal(aj+bjt, σ)
aj=α+γagj+uaj,bj=β+γbgj+ubj
(uajubj)∼MVNormal((00),(τa2ρτaτbρτaτbτb2)).

Two things are new. First, log GDP per person is a group-level predictor: it varies between countries, not within them, and it explains part of the differences in both intercepts and slopes. Second, the country deviations in intercept and slope are drawn jointly from a two-dimensional normal distribution with a correlation ρ, so the model can learn, for example, whether countries that emit more than expected also tend to cut faster. The prior for a correlation matrix is the LKJ distribution (Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe, 2009); LKJ(2) gently favours weak correlations. In brms, (1 + t | country) asks for a correlated varying intercept and slope, and t * g gives the population slope, the effect of income and their interaction (income's effect on the slope).

R
m_co2 <- brm(y ~ 1 + t * g + (1 + t | country), data = co2,
             prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = Intercept),
                       prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
                       prior(exponential(1), class = sd),
                       prior(lkj(2), class = cor),
                       prior(exponential(5), class = sigma)),
             seed = 6, refresh = 0, file = "fits/ch6_co2")
fixef(m_co2) |> round(3)
posterior_summary(m_co2, variable = c("sd_country__Intercept", "sd_country__t",
                                      "cor_country__Intercept__t", "sigma")) |> round(3)
output
          Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5  Q97.5
Intercept    0.672     0.055  0.570  0.789
t            0.105     0.020  0.066  0.144
g            1.205     0.045  1.115  1.291
t:g         -0.163     0.015 -0.192 -0.132
                          Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5 Q97.5
sd_country__Intercept        0.689     0.037  0.623 0.764
sd_country__t                0.235     0.014  0.211 0.264
cor_country__Intercept__t   -0.039     0.075 -0.187 0.106
sigma                        0.120     0.002  0.117 0.123

The population-level results answer the policy question. A country with average income in 2000 emitted about e0.67≈2.0 tonnes of CO₂ per person in 2010, and its emissions per person were rising, by about 11% per decade. Each unit of log GDP per person (a factor of 2.7 in income) multiplied emissions per person by about e1.21≈3.4, and lowered the decade-on-decade slope by about 0.16. So emissions per person were rising in poorer countries and falling in the richest: for a country about 2.7 times richer than the average (one log unit), the slope is roughly 0.11−0.16≈−0.06 per decade.

But countries at the same income level vary enormously around those trends. The standard deviation of country slopes, τb, is about 0.23 per decade: larger than the effect of income itself. And once income is in the model, the correlation between a country's intercept and slope deviations is close to zero. Countries that emit more than their income predicts are not systematically cutting faster or slower; income explained the correlation one would see without it (Exercise 6).

R
show <- c("China", "India", "United States", "United Kingdom", "Brazil", "Nigeria")
nd <- co2 |> filter(country %in% show)
lines_c <- nd |> mutate(fit = fitted(m_co2, newdata = nd)[, "Estimate"],
                        pop = fitted(m_co2, newdata = nd, re_formula = NA)[, "Estimate"])
p1 <- ggplot(lines_c, aes(year, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = harbour[["muted"]], size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = harbour[["sky"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pop), colour = harbour[["amber"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ country, ncol = 3) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2005, 2015)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log tonnes CO2 per person")
fe <- fixef(m_co2)[, "Estimate"]
re_t <- ranef(m_co2)$country[, "Estimate", "t"]                      # country deviations in slope
slopes <- co2 |> distinct(country, g) |>
  mutate(slope = fe["t"] + fe["t:g"] * g + re_t[country])
p2 <- ggplot(slopes, aes(g, slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = harbour[["muted"]]) +
  geom_abline(intercept = fixef(m_co2)["t", 1], slope = fixef(m_co2)["t:g", 1], colour = harbour[["rose"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = harbour[["sky"]], alpha = 0.7, size = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "log GDP per person, 2000 (centred)", y = "slope (log change per decade)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, widths = c(1.5, 1))

The left panel shows partial pooling working on slopes. Each country's solid line uses its own 23 years of data, which dominate here, so the lines follow the points; the dashed line is what the model would predict from income alone, for a new country it had never seen. China's emissions per person rose far faster than its income in 2000 predicted; Nigeria's fell although its income predicted a rise; the United Kingdom fell faster than predicted. With 23 observations per country, shrinkage is mild. With a few observations per country (a new survey of a few hundred firms over three years, say), the same model would pull the noisy country slopes strongly toward the income-predicted line.

One country at a time

Choose a country. Points: its log emissions per person, 2000–2022. Blue: the multilevel trend. Amber dashed: a separate straight line fitted to this country alone (no pooling). Grey dashed: the trend predicted from income in 2000 alone. Use the slider to pretend only the first few years had been observed, and watch how much the multilevel and no-pooling estimates differ when data are scarce. (To refit instantly, the widget holds the population-level parameters, τa, τb, ρ and σ at their posterior means and updates only the chosen country.)

Try four years for China, the United Kingdom and Nigeria. The multilevel line beats the country's own line on the unseen years for the United Kingdom, but not for China, whose emissions rose far faster than countries of its income usually did, or for Nigeria. Pooling helps on average, not in every case. Across all 164 countries, with four years observed, the multilevel trend predicts the remaining 19 years better than the country's own line for about three countries in four, and its root mean squared error is less than half as large (0.30 against 0.68 on the log scale). With ten years observed, the advantage is smaller but still clear (0.31 against 0.37).

Research Practice: Check What the Model Leaves Out

Three limitations of this analysis would be the first questions from a referee in climate economics, and they illustrate questions to ask of any multilevel time-series model.

  • Dependence over time. Residuals from one year to the next are strongly correlated (a bad year is followed by another), but the model treats them as independent, so its intervals for the slopes are too narrow. Chapter 8 adds autocorrelated errors.
  • Measurement. Territorial emissions count CO₂ where it is produced. Rich countries import emission-intensive goods, so consumption-based emissions (also in the Our World in Data file) fall less steeply. The conclusion depends on which you choose; report both.
  • Selection. The analysis uses the 164 countries with complete series and GDP data. Countries without them (often small or in conflict) may differ systematically. Chapter 7 treats missing data.

Check Yourself

The posterior standard deviation of country slopes, τb≈0.23 per decade, is larger than the effect of income on the slope (about 0.16 per log unit). What does this imply?

τ_b measures variation between countries at the same income.

Both quantities are on the same scale (log change per decade).

τb is the spread of country slopes after accounting for income. A typical country's slope differs from its income-predicted slope by about 0.23 per decade, while a full log unit of income (a factor of 2.7) changes the predicted slope by 0.16. Policy, energy mix, industrial structure and other factors matter at least as much.

Countries at the same income level differ in their emission trends by more than income differences explain, so income is far from the whole story.

6.7 The funnel and the non-centred parameterisation

Multilevel models have a computational weak spot that Chapter 5 promised to explain. Consider again the eight countries represented by a single coffee each, but now write the model as Stan code, exactly as the mathematics states it. We draw each country's true average θj directly from Normal(μ,τ): the centred parameterisation.

R
library(rstan)
centred <- "
data { int<lower=1> J; vector[J] ybar; vector<lower=0>[J] se; }
parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> tau; vector[J] theta; }
model {
  mu ~ normal(82, 5); tau ~ exponential(1);
  theta ~ normal(mu, tau);          // centred: country means drawn directly around mu
  ybar ~ normal(theta, se);
}"
noncentred <- "
data { int<lower=1> J; vector[J] ybar; vector<lower=0>[J] se; }
parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> tau; vector[J] z; }
transformed parameters { vector[J] theta = mu + tau * z; }   // non-centred: theta built from z
model {
  mu ~ normal(82, 5); tau ~ exponential(1);
  z ~ normal(0, 1);
  ybar ~ normal(theta, se);
}"
dl <- list(J = nrow(one), ybar = one$mean, se = one$se)
fit_c <- stan(model_code = centred, data = dl, seed = 6, refresh = 0)
fit_n <- stan(model_code = noncentred, data = dl, seed = 6, refresh = 0, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))
divergent <- function(f) sum(sapply(get_sampler_params(f, inc_warmup = FALSE), function(x) sum(x[, "divergent__"])))
tibble(model = c("centred", "non-centred"), divergences = c(divergent(fit_c), divergent(fit_n))) |>
  bind_cols(bind_rows(summary(fit_c, pars = "tau")$summary[, c("mean", "n_eff", "Rhat"), drop = FALSE] |> as_tibble(),
                      summary(fit_n, pars = "tau")$summary[, c("mean", "n_eff", "Rhat"), drop = FALSE] |> as_tibble()))
output
# A tibble: 2 x 5
  model       divergences  mean n_eff  Rhat
  <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 centred             117 1.07   103.  1.05
2 non-centred           0 0.974 2045.  1.00

The centred model produces over a hundred divergent transitions, an R^ of 1.05 for τ and an effective sample size of about a hundred from 4,000 draws. The non-centred model, which is mathematically identical, produces no divergences (with a slightly smaller step size, adapt_delta = 0.95) and an effective sample size twenty times larger. The figure shows why.

R
pc <- as.data.frame(fit_c) |> transmute(log_tau = log(tau), effect = `theta[1]` - mu) |>
  mutate(divergent = unlist(lapply(get_sampler_params(fit_c, inc_warmup = FALSE), function(x) x[, "divergent__"])) == 1,
         model = "centred: theta[1] - mu")
pn <- as.data.frame(fit_n) |> transmute(log_tau = log(tau), effect = `z[1]`, divergent = FALSE,
                                        model = "non-centred: z[1]")
bind_rows(pc, pn) |> group_by(model, divergent) |> slice_head(n = 1500) |> ungroup() |>   # thin for display
  arrange(divergent) |>
  ggplot(aes(effect, log_tau, colour = divergent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = harbour[["sky"]], `TRUE` = harbour[["rose"]]), labels = c("no", "yes")) +
  labs(x = "country effect", y = "log τ", colour = "divergent") + guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))

In the centred parameterisation, the scale of each country effect θj−μ is set by τ. When τ is large the effects can spread widely; when τ is near zero they must all be within a hair of μ. Plotted against log⁡τ, the posterior is a funnel, with a wide mouth at the top and a narrow neck at the bottom. HMC must use one step size for the whole posterior. A step size suited to the wide mouth is far too large for the neck, where the curvature is extreme, so trajectories that try to enter it diverge, and the sampler under-explores small values of τ. This was first described by Radford Neal (2003), and Betancourt and Girolami (2015) analyse its geometry in detail. It is why the centred model's posterior mean for τ came out too high (1.07, against 0.97 from the non-centred model).

The non-centred parameterisation writes each effect as θj=μ+τzj with zj∼Normal(0,1). The model is identical, but the sampler now explores zj, whose scale does not depend on τ, so the funnel becomes a round hill. It is the same trick as centring a predictor in Chapter 5: change coordinates so that the posterior has no extreme curvature. brms uses the non-centred form for every ( | ) term automatically, which is why the coffee and CO₂ models had no divergences. When you write your own Stan models, or when brms still reports divergences, think about the geometry first.

Neal's funnel

A simple funnel: v∼Normal(0,1.5) plays the role of log⁡τ, and θ∼Normal(0,ev). Run HMC with a fixed step size in either parameterisation and plot the draws in the original (θ,v) coordinates. Divergent iterations are red. The dashed line marks the true 5% quantile of v: a sampler that never goes below it has failed to explore the neck.

Check Yourself

Why does the centred parameterisation produce divergences when τ is small?

Small τ is a perfectly plausible value.

The data do not change between parameterisations.

Near τ=0 the conditional distribution of each effect has standard deviation τ, so the density changes extremely fast. HMC's single step size cannot cope with both the wide and the narrow parts, and trajectories in the neck diverge. Non-centring removes the dependence of the effects' scale on τ.

The group effects must then lie in a very narrow region, where the posterior's curvature is far larger than elsewhere, so a step size tuned for the rest of the posterior is too large there.

6.8 A case study: ambulance response times across New York

The techniques of this chapter are made for data like New York City's ambulance dispatch records. The Fire Department publishes every emergency medical incident since 2005 (Fire Department of the City of New York, 2026), more than 30 million of them, on the city's open-data portal, with the call type, a severity code, the borough and ZIP code, and timestamps from the moment the incident is created in the dispatch system to the moment the first unit arrives. We take the most urgent calls of 2024 (severity level 1, which is almost entirely cardiac arrests and choking) and ask a descriptive question: how much does the typical response time vary between the city's ZIP codes, and which ZIP codes are slowest? Some ZIP codes have hundreds of such calls a year and some only a handful, so this is the coffee problem of Section 6.1 with ambulances.

R
url <- paste0("https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/76xm-jjuj.json?",
  "$select=incident_datetime,initial_call_type,borough,zipcode,incident_response_seconds_qy,valid_incident_rspns_time_indc",
  "&$where=initial_severity_level_code='1' AND incident_datetime between '2024-01-01T00:00:00' and '2024-12-31T23:59:59'",
  "&$limit=50000")
ems <- jsonlite::fromJSON(URLencode(url)) |> as_tibble() |>
  filter(valid_incident_rspns_time_indc == "Y", !is.na(zipcode), as.numeric(incident_response_seconds_qy) > 0) |>
  mutate(minutes = as.numeric(incident_response_seconds_qy) / 60, log_min = log(minutes),
         borough = str_to_title(str_remove(borough, "^RICHMOND / ")), date = as.Date(substr(incident_datetime, 1, 10)))
zip_n <- count(ems, zipcode)
c(calls = nrow(ems), zip_codes = nrow(zip_n), min_calls = min(zip_n$n), median_calls = median(zip_n$n), max_calls = max(zip_n$n),
  cardiac_arrest_share = round(mean(ems$initial_call_type == "ARREST"), 3), median_minutes = round(median(ems$minutes), 2))
ems |> group_by(borough) |> summarise(calls = n(), zip_codes = n_distinct(zipcode), median_minutes = round(median(minutes), 2),
                                      over_10_minutes = round(mean(minutes > 10), 3))
output
               calls            zip_codes            min_calls 
           24313.000              192.000                1.000 
        median_calls            max_calls cardiac_arrest_share 
             102.000              404.000                0.911 
      median_minutes 
               5.570 
# A tibble: 5 x 5
  borough       calls zip_codes median_minutes over_10_minutes
  <chr>         <int>     <int>          <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Bronx          5466        25           5.75           0.077
2 Brooklyn       6522        38           5.45           0.058
3 Manhattan      5568        54           5.1            0.059
4 Queens         5503        65           5.97           0.105
5 Staten Island  1254        12           5.68           0.059

After removing the 2% of calls without a valid response time or a ZIP code, there are 24,313 calls in 192 ZIP codes; 91% are cardiac arrests and most of the rest are choking. The citywide median response time is 5.6 minutes. The ZIP codes differ enormously in how much data they provide: the median ZIP code had 102 such calls, the busiest 404 and the smallest one. The boroughs differ modestly: Manhattan has the fastest median (5.1 minutes) and Queens the slowest (6.0 minutes), and in Queens 10.5% of responses took longer than ten minutes, against 6% to 8% elsewhere.

Response times are skewed, with a long right tail of delayed responses, so we model the log of the time in minutes. ZIP codes are nested in boroughs, and both get varying intercepts. Because a few calls in any ZIP code can take far longer than the rest, we use a Student-t likelihood on the log scale (Chapter 3), which lets those calls be unusual without dragging the ZIP estimates:

log⁡(minutesi)∼Student-t(ν, α+bborough[i]+zzip[i], σ),b∼Normal(0,τb),z∼Normal(0,τz).

The prior on α is Normal(1.7, 0.5), centred on about 5.5 minutes, and the group standard deviations have Exponential(5) priors, which put most of their mass on differences between places of less than about 30%.

R
ems_priors <- c(prior(normal(1.7, 0.5), class = Intercept), prior(exponential(5), class = sd),
                prior(exponential(2), class = sigma), prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = nu))
m_ems <- brm(log_min ~ 1 + (1 | borough) + (1 | zipcode), data = ems, family = student(), prior = ems_priors,
             seed = 6, refresh = 0, file = "fits/ch6_ems")
summary(m_ems)$fixed[, c("Estimate", "l-95% CI", "u-95% CI", "Rhat")] |> round(3)
VarCorr(m_ems) |> map(~ round(.x$sd[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")], 3))
summary(m_ems)$spec_pars[, c("Estimate", "l-95% CI", "u-95% CI")] |> round(2)
output
          Estimate l-95% CI u-95% CI  Rhat
Intercept    1.721    1.618    1.822 1.004
$borough
Estimate     Q2.5    Q97.5 
   0.097    0.041    0.220 

$zipcode
Estimate     Q2.5    Q97.5 
   0.129    0.113    0.148 

$residual__
Estimate     Q2.5    Q97.5 
   0.355    0.350    0.360 

      Estimate l-95% CI u-95% CI
sigma     0.35     0.35     0.36

The typical response to a life-threatening call is e1.72≈5.6 minutes (95% interval 5.0 to 6.2). ZIP codes within a borough vary with a standard deviation of 0.13 on the log scale (0.11 to 0.15): a ZIP code one standard deviation slower than its borough's typical one takes about 14% longer, roughly 45 seconds. The borough standard deviation, 0.10, is estimated from only five boroughs and its interval is wide (0.04 to 0.22), the situation Section 6.9's practice box warns about. The Student-t degrees of freedom, ν≈4.5, confirm that the tails are heavy: a normal model on the log scale would have been pulled around by a minority of very long responses. All R^ values are at most 1.004.

R
zip_borough <- distinct(ems, zipcode, borough)
newd <- zip_borough
post_zip <- posterior_linpred(m_ems, newdata = newd)                          # draws x ZIP codes, log minutes
zips <- newd |> mutate(post = exp(apply(post_zip, 2, median)), lo = exp(apply(post_zip, 2, quantile, 0.05)),
                       hi = exp(apply(post_zip, 2, quantile, 0.95))) |>
  left_join(ems |> group_by(zipcode) |> summarise(n = n(), raw = median(minutes)), by = "zipcode")
city <- exp(fixef(m_ems)["Intercept", "Estimate"])
ggplot(zips, aes(n)) + geom_hline(yintercept = city, linetype = 2, colour = harbour[["muted"]]) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n, y = raw, yend = post), colour = harbour[["grid"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(y = raw), shape = 1, colour = harbour[["muted"]], size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = post, colour = borough), size = 1.6) + scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(harbour[c("sky", "rose", "amber", "moss", "lilac")])) +
  labs(x = "life-threatening calls in 2024 (log scale)", y = "typical response time (minutes)", colour = NULL)
bind_rows(zips |> arrange(desc(raw)) |> head(5) |> mutate(ranking = "raw median"),
          zips |> arrange(desc(post)) |> head(5) |> mutate(ranking = "posterior median")) |>
  select(ranking, zipcode, borough, n, raw, post, lo, hi) |> mutate(across(c(raw, post, lo, hi), ~ round(.x, 2))) |> as.data.frame()
output

The figure is Section 6.3's shrinkage plot again, with ambulances. Ranked by their raw medians, three of the five slowest ZIP codes have six calls or fewer, and two have just one: ZIP code 10112 in Midtown Manhattan, which had a single response of 19 minutes, is estimated at 5.4 minutes once it is pooled with the rest of Manhattan. Ranked by posterior medians, the slowest ZIP codes are different and make geographic sense: Breezy Point at the western tip of the Rockaway peninsula (11697: 9.5 minutes, 90% interval 8.4 to 10.7, from 19 calls), followed by Bayside (11360), Howard Beach (11414) and College Point (11356) in Queens and City Island (10464) in the Bronx, all at the edges of the city with limited road access. These estimates rest on enough calls to survive pooling, and they are where an analysis of response-time equity should start looking.

As in Section 6.4, the case for pooling is predictive, and it can be tested: fit the model to the first half of 2024 and predict each ZIP code's typical response in the second half.

R
h1 <- filter(ems, date < as.Date("2024-07-01")); h2 <- filter(ems, date >= as.Date("2024-07-01"))
m_h1 <- update(m_ems, newdata = h1, seed = 6, refresh = 0, file = "fits/ch6_ems_h1")
truth <- h2 |> group_by(zipcode) |> summarise(n2 = n(), target = median(log_min))
raw1 <- h1 |> group_by(zipcode) |> summarise(n1 = n(), raw = median(log_min))
pooled <- zip_borough |> filter(zipcode %in% raw1$zipcode) |>
  mutate(pooled = colMeans(posterior_linpred(m_h1, newdata = zip_borough |> filter(zipcode %in% raw1$zipcode))))
cmp <- truth |> inner_join(raw1, by = "zipcode") |> inner_join(pooled, by = "zipcode")
err <- function(d) c(zip_codes = nrow(d), rmse_raw = sqrt(weighted.mean((d$raw - d$target)^2, d$n2)),
                     rmse_pooled = sqrt(weighted.mean((d$pooled - d$target)^2, d$n2)))
rbind(all = err(cmp), fewer_than_30_calls = err(filter(cmp, n1 < 30)), at_least_30_calls = err(filter(cmp, n1 >= 30))) |> round(3)
output
                    zip_codes rmse_raw rmse_pooled
all                       187    0.097       0.096
fewer_than_30_calls        43    0.184       0.176
at_least_30_calls         144    0.088       0.088

For the 187 ZIP codes with calls in both halves of the year, the pooled estimates predict the second half's typical response slightly better than the raw first-half medians (weighted RMSE on the log scale 0.096 against 0.097). The gain is concentrated where it should be: for the 43 ZIP codes with fewer than 30 calls in the first half, the error falls from 0.184 to 0.176, while for the 144 larger ones the two are identical (0.088). Most ZIP codes have enough calls for their own median to be reliable, so pooling changes little for them; its value here is in protecting rankings, maps and league tables from ZIP codes with a handful of calls, as the raw top five show.

Everything here is descriptive. The model says where responses are slow, not why. Whether neighbourhood composition causes slower responses, the equity question behind this data, is a causal question with the structure of Section 1.9: distance to the nearest ambulance station, traffic, call volume and hospital locations all lie on paths between a neighbourhood and its response times, and some of them are mediators that an equity analysis should not adjust away. A multilevel model like this one is the right outcome model for that analysis; the graph decides what goes into it. Note also what the clock measures: it starts when the incident is created in the dispatch system, after the call has been answered and classified, so any delay before that point is invisible in these data.

6.9 Multilevel models in practice

McElreath (2020) argues that multilevel regression deserves to be the default form of regression, and that a paper should have to justify not using it. Whenever data have clusters (repeated measures on people, students in classes, events in places, measurements over time), single-level models either ignore the clustering, which makes standard errors far too small, or treat each cluster as unrelated, which wastes information and overfits. The models of this chapter extend naturally:

  • Several grouping factors. Students belong to classes and are also assessed by markers; a model with (1 | class) + (1 | marker) has crossed varying effects. Students within classes within schools give nested effects, (1 | school/class).
  • Any likelihood. Varying effects work identically in logistic and Poisson models: recid ~ age + (1 | county) or calls ~ offset(log(pop)) + (1 | neighbourhood).
  • Multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP). To estimate a population quantity from a non-representative sample, such as an opinion poll or the NHANES data of Chapter 3, fit a multilevel model for the outcome by demographic cell and reweight the cell estimates by census counts. MRP is now standard in public opinion research (Gelman and Hill, 2007).

Research Practice: Reporting a Multilevel Model

  • Describe the grouping structure: the number of groups at each level, and the minimum, median and maximum group sizes.
  • Report the group-level standard deviations (and correlations) with intervals, and an intraclass correlation or variance decomposition: they are often the most interesting results.
  • State the priors on the standard deviations, and test sensitivity to them when there are few groups.
  • Show shrinkage (a figure like the one in Section 6.3) and report group-specific estimates with intervals, or rank probabilities, rather than raw rates.
  • Report divergences and the parameterisation used.

Project Connections: Neighbourhoods and Classrooms

Both of your observational projects are multilevel by nature. For emergency medical service in New York, Section 6.8 is the starting point: response times nested in ZIP codes within boroughs, with many ZIP codes having few calls of any one type. The next steps are neighbourhood-level predictors (income, distance to stations, the composition variables of Section 1.9) and a model for all severity levels with varying effects by call type, giving stable estimates and honest rank probabilities. For AI tools in university mathematics, students are nested in sections, sections in courses, and students are crossed with semesters; varying intercepts (and perhaps varying slopes for AI use by course) separate effects that differ across courses from noise, and keep small sections from producing spurious extremes.

Key Takeaways: Lecture 12

  • Varying slopes let each group have its own relationship, drawn with the intercepts from a multivariate normal with an LKJ prior on the correlation.
  • Group-level predictors explain differences between groups; the remaining τ measures what they do not explain.
  • Centred hierarchies create a funnel that causes divergences and biased estimates; the non-centred parameterisation removes it, and brms uses it by default.
  • Make multilevel models your default for clustered data, and report group-level variation as a result in its own right.

6.10 Exercises

Each exercise has a hint and an answer button.

Exercises

  1. One coffee from Japan. From m_coffee, report the posterior mean and 95% interval for the average score of Japanese and Papua New Guinean coffee, and compare them with each country's single observed score. Then compare with Ethiopia.

    coef(m_coffee)$country[c("Japan", "Papua New Guinea", "Ethiopia"), , "Intercept"].

    Japan: posterior mean 82.9 (95% interval 80.5 to 85.5), against its single observed score of 84.7. Papua New Guinea: 83.2 (80.7 to 85.9), against an observed 85.8. Ethiopia: 85.3 (84.6 to 86.0), against an observed average of 85.5 from 44 coffees. Each one-coffee country is pulled about three-quarters of the way to the population mean and keeps an interval about five points wide; Ethiopia barely moves and its interval is under 1.5 points wide. Ethiopia is almost certainly better than both, although their raw scores were higher or similar.

  2. An observation-level predictor. Add the processing method (coded as "Washed / Wet" versus everything else) to the coffee model as a predictor, keeping the country intercepts. Is there evidence that washed coffees score differently? Does τ change?

    Create washed = as.integer(method == "Washed / Wet") (treat missing methods as 0, and say so), then score ~ 1 + washed + (1 | country).

    Of the 1,309 coffees, 812 are washed, 347 are processed in other ways and 150 have no recorded method (coded 0 here; a sensitivity analysis dropping them is a good idea). The coefficient on washed is −0.34 points (95% interval −0.69 to −0.00): washed coffees score slightly lower, by about a seventh of the within-country standard deviation, and the interval only just excludes zero. τ is unchanged (1.43, interval 1.04 to 1.95, against 1.44 before), because processing method varies mostly within countries and so explains almost none of the differences between them. This is an association, not an effect: farms that wash their beans may differ in altitude, variety and other ways.

  3. Variance decomposition. Compute the posterior distribution of the intraclass correlation τ2/(τ2+σ2) for the coffee model. Interpret it in one sentence.

    Use as_draws_df(m_coffee) and the columns sd_country__Intercept and sigma.

    The posterior mean of the intraclass correlation is 0.26, with 95% interval 0.15 to 0.40. About a quarter of the variation in scores lies between countries and three-quarters between coffees from the same country: where a coffee comes from matters, but knowing the country tells you much less about a particular bag than its own tasting does.

  4. Empirical Bayes shrinkage factors. Using μ^, τ^ and σ from the empirical Bayes fit, compute the shrinkage weight wj and the empirical Bayes estimate for every country. Compare the empirical Bayes estimates with the posterior means from m_coffee: what is the largest absolute difference?

    wj=τ^2/(τ^2+σ2/nj) and α^j=μ^+wj(y¯j−μ^).

    With μ^=82.30, τ^=1.41 and σ=2.41, the weights range from 0.26 for the one-coffee countries to 0.99 for Mexico (236 coffees). The United States (8 coffees) has w=0.73 and Haiti (6) has w=0.67. The largest difference between the empirical Bayes estimates and the brms posterior means is 0.045 points (Papua New Guinea); for most countries it is under 0.01. With 36 countries, plugging in τ^ costs almost nothing in the point estimates; the differences that remain are in the widths of the intervals, which empirical Bayes understates.

  5. Shrinking airline safety. Chapter 4 found regression to the mean in airline incident rates. Fit a multilevel Poisson model to the 1985–99 incidents, incidents_85_99 ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure)) + (1 | airline), and use each airline's posterior mean rate to predict its 2000–14 rate. Compare the predictive error with using raw 1985–99 rates and with the overall average rate (after rescaling each period's rates by their mean, since incidents fell overall). Which wins?

    Compare mean((r^1/r^1―−r2/r¯2)2) for the three choices of r^1.

    The model estimates a large spread between airlines in 1985–99 (sd of log rates 1.06, interval 0.84 to 1.35), so it shrinks only modestly. The mean squared errors in predicting the rescaled 2000–14 rates are 2.05 for the raw rates, 2.03 for the multilevel estimates and 1.27 for the flat average: complete pooling wins by a wide margin. The reason is instructive. A multilevel model separates genuine differences from noise under the assumption that the differences are stable; the 1985–99 differences were real, but they did not persist into the next period (airline safety converged as the industry improved). Shrinkage protects against noise, not against change. A model with an airline effect that evolves over time, or a check of how stable group effects are across periods, is needed before using past group rates to rank the future.

  6. Correlation without income. Refit the CO₂ model without the income terms: y ~ 1 + t + (1 + t | country). What is the posterior correlation between country intercepts and slopes now? Explain the difference from m_co2.

    Look at cor_country__Intercept__t.

    Without income, the correlation between country intercepts and slopes is −0.58 (95% interval −0.68 to −0.48), and both standard deviations are larger (τa=1.62, τb=0.31). Countries with high emissions in 2010 tended to have falling emissions. With income in the model the correlation is −0.04 (−0.19 to 0.11). Income in 2000 raises the intercept and lowers the slope, so when it is left out it induces a negative correlation between them; once it is included, the remaining deviations are unrelated. A correlation between varying effects is a description of the groups, not a causal link, and it can change completely when a group-level predictor is added.

  7. Which countries cut fastest?. Using m_co2, compute the posterior probability that the United States, the United Kingdom, China and India each had a negative slope (falling emissions per person) over 2000–2022.

    A country's slope is b_t + b_t:g * g + r_country[country,t], draw by draw.

    Slopes per decade (posterior mean, 95% interval) and the probability that the slope is negative: United Kingdom −0.35 (−0.43 to −0.28), Pr = 1.00; United States −0.19 (−0.27 to −0.12), Pr = 1.00; China +0.45 (0.37 to 0.52), Pr = 0.00; India +0.38 (0.31 to 0.46), Pr = 0.00. Emissions per person fell by about 30% per decade in the United Kingdom and about 18% per decade in the United States, and rose by about 57% and 47% per decade in China and India. Because the model ignores autocorrelation (Section 6.6), these intervals are too narrow, but the signs are not in doubt.

  8. A results paragraph. Write a results paragraph (four or five sentences) for the coffee analysis, following the reporting checklist in Section 6.9.

    Grouping structure, model and priors, τ and σ with intervals, the main finding stated as rank probabilities, and the computation.

    Example. We analysed 1,309 Arabica coffees rated by the Coffee Quality Institute, from 36 countries (median 10.5 coffees per country, range 1 to 236; eight countries contributed a single coffee). Scores were modelled as normal with a varying intercept for country, score∼1+(1∣country), with priors Normal(82, 5) on the mean, Exponential(1) on the between-country standard deviation τ and Exponential(0.5) on the within-country standard deviation σ. Country averages varied with τ=1.44 points (95% CrI 1.02 to 1.97), against σ=2.44 (2.35 to 2.54) within countries, so about a quarter of the variance (ICC 0.26, 0.15 to 0.40) lay between countries. Ethiopia had the highest estimated average (85.3, 84.6 to 86.0) and was the best country in 56% of posterior draws, followed by the United States (31%); no other country exceeded 5%, and countries with a single coffee were shrunk about three-quarters of the way to the overall mean (Figure X). Models were fitted with brms 2.20 and Stan (four chains of 2,000 iterations, 1,000 warmup), with no divergent transitions and R^≤1.01 and bulk ESS above 500 for all parameters.

Further reading and references

Further Reading

  • McElreath, Statistical Rethinking (2nd ed., 2020), Chapters 13–14: varying intercepts and slopes, the non-centred parameterisation, and the case for multilevel models as the default.
  • Gelman and Hill, Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (2007): the classic applied treatment, including the radon example and MRP.
  • Efron, Large-Scale Inference (2010): empirical Bayes for thousands of simultaneous estimates, from the person who popularised Stein's paradox.
  • Efron and Morris, "Stein's paradox in statistics" (Scientific American, 1977): the most readable introduction to shrinkage ever written.
  • Betancourt and Girolami, "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for hierarchical models" (2015): the geometry of funnels and why non-centring works.
